content: Amnioinfusion is a medical procedure designed to prevent or alleviate umbilical cord compression during labor by introducing a fluid into the uterine cavity. This intervention is intended to improve outcomes for both the mother and the baby. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of amnioinfusion on maternal and perinatal outcomes in cases of potential or suspected umbilical cord compression during labor. The researchers conducted a systematic review of randomized trials comparing amnioinfusion to no amnioinfusion in women whose babies were at risk of umbilical cord compression. The review included 19 studies, most of which had fewer than 200 participants. Transcervical amnioinfusion was associated with several significant benefits. It reduced the overall rate of cesarean sections (based on 13 trials with 1,493 participants, with a risk ratio of 0.62 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.46 to 0.83). It also decreased the occurrence of fetal heart rate decelerations (seven trials, 1,006 participants; risk ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.74). Additionally, it lowered the likelihood of an Apgar score below seven at five minutes after birth (12 trials, 1,804 participants; risk ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.72) and reduced the presence of meconium below the vocal cords (three trials, 674 participants; risk ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.92). Maternal outcomes also improved with transcervical amnioinfusion. The risk of postpartum endometritis was reduced (six trials, 767 participants; risk ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.81), as was the likelihood of a maternal hospital stay exceeding three days (four trials, 1,051 participants; risk ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.78). Transabdominal amnioinfusion demonstrated similar trends, but the number of participants in these studies was smaller, limiting the strength of the conclusions. The mean umbilical artery pH was higher in the amnioinfusion group (seven trials, 855 participants; mean difference 0.03, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.06). There was also a trend toward fewer neonates with a low cord arterial pH (defined as less than 7.2 or as specified by the trial authors) in the amnioinfusion group (eight trials, 972 participants; risk ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.14). The authors concluded that amnioinfusion for potential or suspected umbilical cord compression may provide significant benefits for both the mother and the baby. These benefits include a reduction in variable fetal heart rate decelerations, improved short-term neonatal outcomes, a lower risk of maternal postpartum endometritis, and a decreased rate of cesarean sections. However, the trials reviewed had methodological limitations, and the sample sizes were too small to assess the risk of rare but serious maternal adverse effects. Further research is needed to confirm these findings, evaluate long-term fetal outcomes, and determine the impact of amnioinfusion on cesarean section rates when the diagnosis of fetal distress is more rigorously defined. Future studies should also investigate the use of amnioinfusion in specific clinical scenarios, such as fetal heart rate decelerations, oligohydramnios, or prelabor rupture of membranes.
